newsitem.title: UK: UK funds 40 bln stg short in top shares-Schroders.
newsitem.headline: UK funds 40 bln stg short in top shares-Schroders.

text.p: British investment institutions would have to spend 40 billion stg to correct their major underweight positions in some of this year's top performing shares, according to a study released on Thursday by Schroders.

Having missed out on sharp gains in blue chip UK bank and drug stocks, domestic funds run the risk of further underperformance from their underweight positions in the likes of HSBC Holdings Plc and SmithKline Beecham Plc, according to Schroders.
Reversing these underweight positions will not be easy, according to Schroders equity strategist, Paul Walton.

Yet the recent technical squeeze in top performing shares could be exacerbated by trends towards greater indexation, U.S. enthusiasm for UK shares and share buybacks diminishing the supply of equity, he said.
Based on an analysis of the ownership of UK shares, the Schroders study aims to reveal underlying trends in actual investment strategy being pursued by fund managers.

It is another indication of the problems caused for many fund managers, wedded to traditional valuation techniques, caused by the recent outperformance of a handful of top shares such as Lloyds TSB Plc and Glaxo Wellcome Plc.

Many funds have underperformed because they have been overweight in high-yielding stocks which looked good value but have lagged the FTSE 100 index as it hit a succession of record highs, Walton said.

Some market participants believe UK institutions have not adjusted quickly enough to the current low-inflation environment where outperformance has come from "growth" stocks offering the prospect of expanding profits and future dividend growth.
"There is a clear case of over-ownership in high yield/high dividend payout shares by domestic funds," the report argued.
"Domestic funds are too exposed to a high 'running yield' rather than to income (or dividend) growth. We think funds should look for a better combination of yield and dividend growth."

The analysis found the largest underweight positions in HSBC, where funds were two percent or 11 billion stg short of a market weighting, and SmithKline Beecham, where the underweight position was one percent or 5.5 billion stg.
Other major underweight positions were in Halifax, Glaxo, British Petroleum Co Plc, British Telecom, Reuters Holdings Plc and British Sky Broadcasting Plc.

"The scale of buying required to neutralise this position is massive," the study said. "We estimate that it would cost over 40 billion stg, some 5.5 percent of the outstanding value of UK equity holdings or around two thirds of present free cash balances."

"There is an argument that 'chasing' these stocks after a period of outperformance is the wrong thing to do, although having done fundamental work on why big stocks are outpacing smaller stocks we would disagree."

The report also highlighted recent buying by U.S. investment funds particularly in "cyclical" shares, saying they had built up dominant positions in the likes of British Steel Plc, BTR Plc and Imperial Chemical Industries Plc.

"We think this 'contrarian' approach is too early, but it is nonetheless an interesting sign of how hard it might be for UK funds to get exposure to certain stocks when the time is right," Walton said.
